summary_html: **Educators/school staff** observing indicators of abuse/neglect report to CPS under state mandatory-reporter lists built on the federal CAPTA floor.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — requires robust reporter regimes that include education sector professionals

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary disposition for a physician sued for failing to report suspected abuse of another child, holding the Child Protection Law creates a private remedy only for the identified abused child and that no common-law duty ran to a later-injured third party.
key_cases.relevance: School staff who fail to report face the statute's criminal and civil provisions, but their civil exposure runs only to the identified child.
key_cases.quote: Michigan's child abuse reporting statute creates a private right of action only in an identified abused child.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that an employer may be vicariously liable for an employee's failure to report under MCL 722.623 and that the Child Protection Law's good-faith immunity in MCL 722.625 does not extend to negligence or medical malpractice; the Supreme Court denied leave.
key_cases.relevance: The same employer-liability reasoning reaches institutions whose staff are mandated reporters, including schools.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that an employer may be held liable for its employee's failure to report under MCL 722.623

key_cases.case_name: Brent v Wayne County Department of Human Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held Michigan's Child Protection Law immunity is an immunity from suit that is immediately appealable, granted state defendants absolute immunity for conduct connected to preparing and filing the removal petition, and reversed dismissal of certain § 1983 and gross-negligence claims.
key_cases.relevance: Institutional reporters, including school and hospital staff, can invoke the immunity and appeal immediately if it is denied.
key_cases.quote: We therefore conclude, like the Court in Forsyth, that the entitlement under Martin "is an immunity from suit rather than a mere defense to liability."

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the Fourteenth Amendment claims, holding that a safety plan excuses the state from affording a parent process only where the parent's consent is voluntary and free of duress, and it reversed on the Fourth Amendment claims while holding prospectively that a social worker needs at least reasonable suspicion of abuse to conduct an in-school interview without a warrant or consent.
key_cases.relevance: The Court held the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child in an abuse investigation, requiring at least reasonable suspicion absent a warrant or consent, which directly constrains how a school-based disclosure may be followed up.
key_cases.quote: The only exception to this rule is when a parent voluntarily consents to the terms of a safety plan without duress.

search_keywords: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, dentists, physician's assistants, registered dental hygienists, medical examiners, nurses, and persons licensed to provide emergency medical care — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(a)
Audiologists, psychologists, physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and athletic trainers

Marriage and family therapists, licensed professional counselors, social workers, licensed master's social workers, licensed bachelor's social workers, registered social service technicians, and social service technicians
Persons employed in a professional capacity in any office of the friend of the court
School administrators, school counselors, and teachers

MDHHS eligibility specialists, family independence managers, family independence specialists, social services specialists, social work specialists, social work specialist managers, and welfare services specialists — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(b)
Employees of an organization that federal funding statutes, regulations, or contracts would otherwise bar from reporting absent a state mandate — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(c)
Not universal: any other person, including a child, MAY report but is not required to — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624
reporting_details: Michigan is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals and MDHHS employees listed in Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1) must report, and they must report immediately to MDHHS centralized intake by telephone or through the Michigan Online Reporting System. A telephone report must be followed within 72 hours by a written report on form DHS-3200, faxed or emailed to Centralized Intake; a report filed through the online reporting system that contains the information required by Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(2) counts as the written report, and MDHHS states that reporting online eliminates the requirement to fill out a DHS-3200 form. Any other person may report voluntarily under Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: MDHHS centralized intake receives the report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.628(1) requires the department, within 24 hours of receiving a report, to refer it to the prosecuting attorney and local law enforcement or to commence an investigation.
Not specified; MDHHS states CPS has 30 days to complete an investigation unless extenuating circumstances require an extension.
